newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FEATURE - Uphill run for Swedish ski resort share.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Uphill run for Swedish ski resort share.

text.p: Although the idea of listing a mountain ski resort may seem strange to some, Swedes are gradually warming to the idea.
Shares in the popular ski spot of Lindvallen, 450 km (280 miles) northwest of Stockholm, have risen 100 percent since Feburary.
On December 10 -- the last time it was traded -- the share, whose full company name is Lindvallen i Salen AB, closed at 60 crowns ($8.81).
Listed on the Stockholm bourse in July 1994, the share price is exposed to factors ranging from competition from charter holidays to cheaper, sunnier places or mother nature herself.
"Our main competitors are beach and golf vacations," managing director Thorvald Sverdrup told Reuters.
To keep Swedes on the slopes, Sverdrup is banking partly on the fact that Scandinavians are avid skiers.

A survey by industry organisation Svenska Liftanlaggningars showed that 1.7 million Swedes skied last year and that out of a population of 8.8 million, 1.9 million planned to ski in the 1996/97 season.
SIMPLICITY IS KEY
Another tactic is to simplify the ski holiday, offering it as a convenient package including lift tickets and accommodation.

The resort, which has sleeping capacity for 10,000 in the direct vicinity of its lifts including 4,400 beds in its own facilities, has restaurants, conference facilities, shops, a gym and a bowling alley.

This season will see the debut of watches which contain a chip that can be programmed for the length of a guest's stay. Held in front of a special sensor at the entrance of the ski lifts, the gate opens and allows the skier to pass.
The watch is environmentally-friendly because it replaces disposable plastic lift cards and is easier to use.

Lindvallen, which has 40 percent market share among other resorts in Salen, also hopes to draw more foreigners by marketing Sweden's exotic reputation abroad. The nearest airport, at Mora is about 90 minutes away by taxi.

"I believe in the coming winter we have plans for charters from Britain directly to Mora airport. If you're leaving from London, travel times aren't that much different than to other ski areas in Europe," Sverdrup said.
SNOW A SIGNIFICANT SHARE FACTOR
Some analysts are wary of the share because of the company's volatile profits from year to year.
"Every now and then you don't have any snow and they don't have any profit," said one Stockholm-based analyst.
Sverdrup said this problem was countered by computerised cannons which blast artificial snow onto the piste and insulate the share from changes in the weather.
The resort has a long season -- until May 1 -- because of its northerly location and sold 690,000 one-day lift passes in the 1995/96 ski season.
"Last winter was the worst one in 70 years. All of the skiing was based on man-made snow. We showed the share market that we could keep the profit level up even in such a season."

In the 1995/96 fiscal year ending August 31 it posted a profit of 33.1 million crowns after financial net on turnover of 143 million crowns. This compared to a profit of 32.9 million crowns on turnover of 131.9 million crowns the year before.

"I expect turnover to increase by eight to 10 percent this year," Sverdrup said, adding that he expected the resort's accommodation to be about 95 percent booked compared to 90 percent during the 1995/96 winter season.
Other analysts note the steady development of the profit growth even in the depths of the 1990s recession.
WORLD'S FIRST MCSKI
Lindvallen has teamed up with McDonald's, opening the world's first ski-through restaurant where skiers can order hamburgers and fries through a special window and ski off.
Lindvallen has invested 250 million crowns in the past four years, including 55 million crowns ahead of this year's season, partly towards a six-seat chair lift.

Sverdrup said adding more leisure sector shares to the Stockholm bourse could boost interest in Lindvallen, whose turnover averaged 48,000 crowns a day in the third quarter of 1996, making it one of the smaller stocks on the Stockholm bourse.

Swedish investment, health care and information technology company Investment AB Bure is in talks to buy holding company Are Invest AB -- the owner of the rival ski resort of Are -- and has said it is considering listing Are in a few years.
The hotel chain Scandic Hotels is due to be listed this month.
"We are the only tourist oriented share on the market and this is a problem," Sverdrup said. "We need three to four more companies." ($1=6.810 Swedish Crown)
